problems.name: Integer multiplication
problems.summary: How efficiently can we multiply two enormous whole numbers?
problems.why: Multiplication is a basic ingredient in computing. This research asks about the ultimate growth of the work needed as numbers get longer.
problems.opportunity: Increase the saving in the logarithmic exponent while keeping the same exact, fixed-tape computation model.

metric.label: Logarithmic saving
metric.explanation: A larger κ means a stronger theoretical saving. It does not measure how much faster a computer runs today.

problems.assumptions: Two n-bit integers, exact output, deterministic worst-case time on one fixed finite-alphabet machine with finitely many one-dimensional tapes. Constants and machine are fixed before inputs vary.
problems.formalizationScope: The catalogue does not list an accompanying top-line Lean formalization for this multiplication claim.

papers.title: Integer multiplication below n log n

problems.publishedSummary: Multiplies two n-bit integers exactly at every input length in deterministic worst-case time $`O(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa})`$, with $`\kappa=2^{-182}`$, on one fixed finite-alphabet Turing machine with finitely many one-dimensional tapes. This disproves the Schönhage–Strassen $`n\log n`$ optimality conjecture in the ordinary multitape bit model.

problems.name: Fourier transforms
problems.summary: Can we break a signal into its frequencies with fewer mathematical operations?
problems.why: Fourier transforms are central to signal processing. These papers study exact arithmetic and the asymptotic growth of operation counts.
problems.opportunity: Increase the saving δ, accounting for every operation and any extra logarithmic factors.

metric.label: Logarithmic saving
metric.explanation: Larger δ is a better asymptotic exponent. Exact complex arithmetic is different from a practical finite-precision FFT.

problems.assumptions: Every positive transform length, exact complex arithmetic, unrestricted coefficients, and a supplied root of unity. Scalar preparation and logarithmic-word indexing are counted; finite-precision stability and bit complexity are different questions.
problems.formalizationScope: The upstream notes report a uniform all-length 10⁻¹³ theorem and a separate subsequential circuit theorem. The latter alone would not imply an all-length algorithm; extraction/search uniformization is outside the selected statements.

papers.title: An explicit power saving for the exact discrete Fourier transform
Finite tensor savings and exact Fourier circuits

problems.publishedSummary: Gives a deterministic length-n discrete Fourier transform algorithm using $`O(n(\log n)^{1-\delta})`$ operations for every n, with explicit $`\delta=10^{-13}`$. The model uses exact complex arithmetic, unrestricted coefficients and a supplied root of unity, and counts scalar preparation and logarithmic-word indexing. ([Lean](lean/docs/130.md))

problems.name: Matrix multiplication
problems.summary: How much work does it take to multiply two large grids of numbers?
problems.why: Matrix multiplication sits inside scientific computing and machine learning. The exponent describes how arithmetic grows with grid size.
problems.opportunity: Lower the exponent, or extend a bound to more kinds of numbers. Compare results over the same field.

metric.label: Arithmetic exponent
metric.explanation: Smaller ω means a stronger asymptotic arithmetic-complexity bound. The October headline applies to complex numbers.

problems.assumptions: Square matrix multiplication over ℂ in division-free arithmetic programs, allowing every fixed positive exponent slack ε. This is an arithmetic-operation bound, not a bit-operation or benchmark bound.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report ω(ℂ) ≤ 9/4, plus separate rectangular and all-field bounds. Their all-field result is < 2.371054886006746; it does not by itself establish 9/4 over every field.

papers.title: An Upper Bound of 9/4 for the Matrix Multiplication Exponent
Complex Matrix Multiplication Below 2.258 and Rectangular Bounds
Staggered extraction for exact matrix multiplication over every field

problems.publishedSummary: Proves $`\omega\le9/4`$ over ℂ, giving $`O_\varepsilon(n^{9/4+\varepsilon})`$ arithmetic operations for square matrix multiplication. In characteristic zero, some inner dimension na with a > 0.465 permits $`n^{2+o(1)}`$ rectangular multiplication. Further square bounds give ω < 2.258 outside finitely many positive characteristics and ω < 2.371054886006746 over every fixed field. ([Lean](lean/docs/107.md))

problems.name: Zero-free regions
problems.summary: How far can we push the region where certain functions are guaranteed never to equal zero?
problems.why: The zeros of these functions are connected to the distribution of prime numbers. A smaller boundary rules out zeros in a larger region.
problems.opportunity: Lower the right-hand boundary of the zero-free half-plane, preserving the same class of functions.

metric.label: Zero-free boundary
metric.explanation: Smaller β widens the zero-free region. Improving this bound is not the same as proving the Riemann hypothesis.

problems.assumptions: The strict half-plane Re(s) > β for Dirichlet L-functions and finite-order Hecke L-functions over ℚ(√−3). Principal-character poles at s = 1 are excluded. No claim is made about the boundary line.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report 7/8 bounds for zeta, Dirichlet, and the specified Hecke functions. This dashboard has not compiled or audited their theorem dependencies.

papers.title: The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: A Zero-Free Half-Plane \Re s> 7/8
The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis (alternate 11/12 proof)
Uniform exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeros

problems.publishedSummary: Proves that every Dirichlet L-function, including $`\zeta(s)`$, is zero-free in $`\Re s\gt 7/8`$, resolving the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. The same half-plane is zero-free for every finite-order Hecke L-function over $`\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})`$. A companion gives a different proof of the zero-free half-plane $`\Re s\gt 11/12`$. ([Lean](lean/docs/003.md))

problems.name: Heilbronn triangles
problems.summary: Place points in a square so that even the smallest triangle stays as large as possible.
problems.why: This is a simple geometric puzzle with very difficult guarantees. The goal is to keep every triangle formed by three points from being too tiny.
problems.opportunity: Find a larger positive saving η with a valid construction for every sufficiently large number of points.

metric.label: Triangle-area saving
metric.explanation: A larger η gives a stronger lower bound on the smallest triangle. The catalogue states a positive saving without a numeric headline.

problems.assumptions: The manuscript claim concerns n points in the unit square and all sufficiently large n, with one fixed positive area-exponent saving. It is an asymptotic construction, not a finite point-set record.
problems.formalizationScope: The reported Lean statement covers an unbounded sequence of sizes. The manuscript’s every-sufficiently-large-n claim is broader; the existence of the linked formalization does not certify that broader scope.

papers.title: A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound

problems.publishedSummary: For every sufficiently large n, constructs n points in the unit square such that every triangle has area at least $`n^{-2+c}`$ for one absolute c > 0. This disproves the conjectured almost-n−2 upper bound in Heilbronn's triangle problem, which asks how large the smallest determined triangle can be. ([Lean](lean/docs/191.md))

problems.name: Job scheduling
problems.summary: Finish jobs as quickly as possible when some jobs must wait for others.
problems.why: The released manuscript claims optimal schedules for unit-length jobs on three identical machines, including arbitrary dependencies.
problems.opportunity: Explore whether the exact guarantee extends to more machines, while checking that the algorithm really finds an optimal schedule.

metric.label: Machines covered
metric.explanation: Here the frontier is the scope of the guarantee: how many machines it covers. A proposed four-machine adaptation still needs careful review.

problems.assumptions: Nonpreemptive unit-length jobs with arbitrary acyclic precedence constraints on three identical parallel machines. The objective is minimum makespan, and the input explicitly encodes the precedence graph.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report exact deadline feasibility and optimal schedules for nonempty instances in polynomial binary-input time. Four-machine adaptations require their own completeness and optimality arguments.

papers.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Three-Machine Unit-Job Scheduling

problems.publishedSummary: Resolves the three-processor unit-job scheduling problem of Garey and Johnson: a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm minimizes makespan for nonpreemptive unit-length jobs with arbitrary precedence constraints on three identical parallel machines. For an explicitly given precedence graph, it decides deadline feasibility exactly and constructs a feasible schedule. ([Lean](lean/docs/124.md))

problems.name: Subset Sum
problems.summary: Choose some numbers from a list so that they add up to an exact target.
problems.why: This classic problem appears in combinatorial search. A smaller exponent reduces the theoretical growth of a worst-case search.
problems.opportunity: Lower the runtime exponent below 0.49 under the same randomized word-RAM guarantees.

metric.label: Exponential-time exponent
metric.explanation: Smaller α means a better exponential runtime bound. The guarantee includes a success probability of at least two thirds.

problems.assumptions: Worst-case lists of positive integers, including repeats, with polynomial-bit inputs. Randomized word-RAM time is bounded on every execution; success is at least 2/3 per input, with O(n+b)-bit words.
problems.formalizationScope: The catalogue does not list an accompanying top-line Lean formalization for this Subset Sum claim.

papers.title: Subset Sum in Time O(2^{0.49n})
A Low-Space Algorithm for Worst-Case Subset Sum

problems.publishedSummary: Gives a uniform randomized classical algorithm for worst-case Subset Sum in ordinary $`O(2^{0.49n})`$ word-RAM time on polynomial-bit inputs, where n counts the integers. The time bound holds on every execution and success probability is at least 2/3 on every input. Inputs may repeat positive integers; words have $`O(n+b)`$ bits for maximum input bit length b.

problems.name: Matroid prophet inequalities
problems.summary: Choose valuable options as they arrive, with limited capacity and no undo button.
problems.why: You get one historical sample per option. The guarantee compares your expected total reward with the best feasible selection made by someone who sees all values in advance.
problems.opportunity: Raise the guaranteed fraction while retaining one sample, arbitrary finite matroids and an adversary that sees every sample, value and random seed.

metric.label: Guaranteed reward fraction
metric.explanation: Larger α guarantees a greater fraction of the expected hindsight optimum. This is a theorem coefficient, not observed performance or a polynomial-time implementation.

problems.assumptions: Every finite labeled matroid known in advance; independent nonnegative element values with one independent identically distributed sample per element. Only the expected offline optimum must be finite. Choices are irrevocable and feasible after every arrival prefix. The arrival order may depend measurably on all samples, values and the complete finite random seed; computation and storage need not be polynomial.
problems.formalizationScope: The release notes report a one-sample prophet guarantee of 2⁻³¹⁰ and a separate fixed-weight hidden-vector selection guarantee of 2⁻²⁹³. The latter alone is not the one-sample theorem. This app has not independently compiled or checked the Lean dependencies.

papers.title: One Sample Suffices for Matroid Prophet Inequalities against an Almighty Adversary

problems.publishedSummary: For every finite matroid known in advance, gives a distribution-independent online rule using one independent sample per element and earning a universal constant fraction of the expected offline optimum. Values are independent and nonnegative, with finite expected optimum. The guarantee holds even when the arrival-order adversary sees all samples, values, and the rule's entire random seed; no polynomial-time implementation is asserted. ([Lean](lean/docs/111.md))

problems.name: Time-to-space simulation
problems.summary: Simulate a long computation while using much less memory.
problems.why: A simulation can trade a great deal of time for less storage. This result concerns the memory needed to recover a machine’s outcome.
problems.opportunity: Lower the power of T in the space bound, preserving the one-tape model and input-access assumptions.

metric.label: Space exponent
metric.explanation: A smaller a means less asymptotic memory. This theorem does not promise a faster simulation.

problems.assumptions: A fixed deterministic machine with one writable tape and finitely many read-only input heads; head moves are local, initial contents are independent of T, and symbols have polylogarithmic-space access. Simulation time is unrestricted.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report finite-control and halting outcomes in two-fifths-power space. General multitape simulations and hierarchy consequences are outside the selected statements.

papers.title: Simulating One-Tape Time in Two-Fifths-Power Space

problems.publishedSummary: Determines the halting and finite-control outcome of a fixed deterministic one-writable-tape machine up to time T using $`O(T^{2/5}\log^C(T+2))`$ space, improving the square-root exponent. Heads move at most one cell per step; finitely many read-only input heads are allowed. Initial contents are independent of T, and contents and input symbols have polylogarithmic-space access. Simulation time is unrestricted. ([Lean](lean/docs/137.md))

problems.name: Permanent lower bounds
problems.summary: Prove that a certain difficult calculation cannot be represented by a small determinant.
problems.why: Lower bounds tell us what computation cannot avoid. The permanent looks like a determinant but behaves very differently.
problems.opportunity: Raise the exponent in the border determinantal complexity lower bound, keeping the same representation model.

metric.label: Lower-bound exponent
metric.explanation: Larger a proves a stronger limitation. This is a lower bound on representation size, not an algorithm speedup.

problems.assumptions: The complex n×n permanent, represented by determinants of affine-linear matrices or coefficientwise limits of such representations. The lower bound holds asymptotically for matrix size.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report cubic exact and border determinantal lower bounds, including an explicit threshold. Broader algebraic-branching-program consequences are outside those statements.

papers.title: A cubic lower bound for border determinantal complexity of the permanent

problems.publishedSummary: Proves an $`\Omega(n^3)`$ lower bound for the border determinantal complexity of the $`n\times n`$ permanent over ℂ. Even coefficientwise limits of determinants of affine-linear matrices require matrix size at least $`cn^3`$, for an absolute c > 0 and all sufficiently large n; the same bound therefore holds for exact representations. ([Lean](lean/docs/108.md))

problems.name: Strategy games
problems.summary: Find the best strategy in games played on a network of states.
problems.why: These games are used to reason about systems that interact over time. The release gives quasipolynomial algorithms with precisely stated input models.
problems.opportunity: Improve the time bound toward polynomial time, without dropping reward, probability, or priority encodings.

metric.label: Algorithmic growth
metric.explanation: This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, not a polynomial-time guarantee. Hidden constants prevent a direct numeric comparison.

problems.assumptions: The manuscript’s deterministic quasipolynomial bit-time claim uses complete binary input length L, including signed rewards, rational probabilities, and priorities. Its ordinary, stochastic, and parity variants have distinct output guarantees.
problems.formalizationScope: The reported Lean scope is a randomized ordinary mean-payoff winning-set algorithm with success ≥ 7/8, plus a finite counterexample. It does not certify the deterministic and extended-game claims shown in the family description.

papers.title: Turn-Based Stochastic Mean-Payoff Games in Deterministic Quasipolynomial Time
Mean-payoff parity games in quasipolynomial time
Deterministic quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games
Randomized quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games

problems.publishedSummary: Gives deterministic algorithms using $`2^{O((\log(L+2))^2)}`$ bit operations, for complete binary input length L, for ordinary mean-payoff games and two separate extensions. They compute exact values and optimal positional strategies in ordinary games, the nonnegative expectation-of-liminf value set in turn-based stochastic games, and the winning set for nonnegative liminf mean payoff conjoined with parity. Signed rewards, rational chance probabilities, and parity priorities are unrestricted and binary-encoded. ([Lean](lean/docs/104.md))

problems.name: Exact graph matching
problems.summary: Pair as many connected points as possible without using a point twice.
problems.why: Matching appears in assignment and network problems. The released manuscript describes a randomized exact algorithm with almost-linear word time.
problems.opportunity: Improve the remaining overhead or reliability while retaining an exact maximum matching.

metric.label: Runtime overhead
metric.explanation: The o(1) term tends to zero as the graph grows. A concrete overhead bound is needed before a numeric improvement can be ranked.

problems.assumptions: Simple undirected graphs, exact maximum-cardinality matching, randomized word time, and success at least 2/3. The time bound holds on every computation path.
problems.formalizationScope: The catalogue does not list an accompanying top-line Lean formalization for this matching claim.

papers.title: Almost-Linear-Time Maximum-Cardinality Matching in General Graphs

problems.publishedSummary: Gives a randomized algorithm finding an exact maximum-cardinality matching in any simple undirected graph in $`(n+m)^{1+o(1)}`$ word time, with success probability at least 2/3. The time bound holds on every computation path. The same guarantees apply to finding a spanning subgraph with prescribed admissible vertex degrees, or deciding that none exists.

problems.name: Edit distance
problems.summary: Estimate how many insertions, deletions, or changes turn one string into another.
problems.why: Comparing sequences is useful across computing. The manuscript claims almost-linear expected time for any fixed relative approximation error.
problems.opportunity: Improve runtime overhead, accuracy dependence, or success guarantees while holding the other parameters fixed.

metric.label: Runtime overhead
metric.explanation: Accuracy is fixed before the asymptotic comparison. Bounds with different accuracy settings are not directly comparable.

problems.assumptions: Unit-cost edit distance, fixed rational relative error ε ∈ (0,1), total length N, and polynomially bounded integer symbols. The approximation succeeds with probability at least 2/3; the time guarantee is expected time.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report a randomized (1+ε) estimate in expected almost-linear work at fixed accuracy. This is not an exact-distance or deterministic worst-case-time claim.

papers.title: An Almost-Linear Approximation Scheme for Edit Distance

problems.publishedSummary: For every fixed rational $`\varepsilon\in(0,1)`$, gives a randomized $`(1+\varepsilon)`$ approximation to unit-cost edit distance in worst-case expected time $`N^{1+o(1)}`$, with success probability at least 2/3. The strings have total length N and polynomially bounded integer symbols. This is an asymptotic guarantee at fixed accuracy. ([Lean](lean/docs/121.md))

problems.name: Deletion-trace reconstruction
problems.summary: Reconstruct a string from many copies in which some characters have disappeared.
problems.why: How many damaged copies are enough? The release leaves a gap between a superpolynomial lower bound and a quasipolynomial reconstruction bound.
problems.opportunity: Close the gap in the number of samples needed, for the same deletion probability.

metric.label: Samples required
metric.explanation: Stronger upper bounds need fewer samples; stronger lower bounds prove more are necessary. Keep these two directions separate.

problems.assumptions: Worst-case binary strings, independent deletion traces, and a fixed deletion probability in (0,1). Upper and lower sample bounds answer different questions; the uniform decoder upper bound assumes a known fixed rational retention probability.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report superpolynomial and quantitative sample lower bounds. The family’s quasipolynomial decoder upper bound is outside the selected formalized statement.

papers.title: Uniform quasipolynomial-time trace reconstruction
A latest-anchor induction with spectrally compact masks for worst-case trace reconstruction
Quantitative lower bounds for trace reconstruction

problems.publishedSummary: At every fixed deletion probability in $`(0,1)`$, reconstructing an arbitrary length-n binary string requires $`n^{\Omega(\log\log n)}`$ independent traces, ruling out polynomial-sample reconstruction. A uniform decoder achieves quasipolynomial sample and running-time bounds for known fixed rational retention probabilities. When the deletion probability is at most $`n^{-\varepsilon}`$ for fixed ε > 0, both bounds become polynomial in the input and parameter encoding. ([Lean](lean/docs/122.md))

problems.name: Arithmetic progressions
problems.summary: How many numbers can a set contain while avoiding a fixed-length equal-step pattern?
problems.why: Dense sets are forced to contain structure. Quantitative bounds measure how strong that guarantee can be.
problems.opportunity: Increase the decay exponent εₖ for a fixed progression length k, with explicit constants and assumptions.

metric.label: Density-decay exponent
metric.explanation: A larger exponent gives a stronger size restriction. The catalogue does not specify its numerical value.

problems.assumptions: A nonconstant k-term arithmetic progression with fixed k ≥ 3, and subsets of {1,…,N}. The positive constants and decay exponent depend on k; changing k changes the comparison.
problems.formalizationScope: The reported Lean statement is the divergent-reciprocal-sum consequence. The quantitative progression-free-set upper bound displayed here is outside that selected statement.

papers.title: Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions

problems.publishedSummary: Proves Erdős's conjecture that every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. Quantitatively, for each fixed k ≥ 3, every subset of $`\{1,\ldots,N\}`$ with no nonconstant k-term progression has size at most $`C_kN\exp[-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}]`$, with positive constants depending only on k. ([Lean](lean/docs/159.md))

problems.name: Van der Waerden numbers
problems.summary: Colour the number line while avoiding a long equal-step pattern of one colour.
problems.why: Lower bounds say how long an interval can remain free of a monochromatic pattern.
problems.opportunity: Strengthen the growth constant or construction for specified numbers of colours and pattern lengths.

metric.label: Growth constant
metric.explanation: Larger c gives a stronger lower bound. Colour count and progression length must be held consistent.

problems.assumptions: For every integer colour count r ≥ 2 and all sufficiently large progression lengths k, with one absolute threshold independent of r. Wᵣ(k) is the least interval length forcing a monochromatic k-term progression.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report the uniform lower bound with c = 1/100000, its growth limits, and boundary values. Sharper intermediate estimates are excluded. The catalogue headline itself states only c > 0.

papers.title: Quantitative Superexponential Bounds for van der Waerden Numbers

problems.publishedSummary: Resolves Erdős's superexponential-growth question for van der Waerden numbers. If $`W_r(k)`$ is the least interval length forcing a monochromatic k-term progression in every r-coloring, then $`W_r(k)\gt k^{ck\lfloor\log_2 r\rfloor}`$ for an absolute c > 0, all r ≥ 2 and sufficiently large k, uniformly in r. In particular, $`W_r(k)^{1/k}\to\infty`$ for each fixed r. ([Lean](lean/docs/160.md))

problems.name: Planar unit distances
problems.summary: How many pairs of points in the plane can sit exactly one unit apart?
problems.why: A stronger counting bound limits how frequently one distance can occur in a point arrangement.
problems.opportunity: Increase the power saving δ in the bound on the number of unit-distance pairs.

metric.label: Counting-exponent saving
metric.explanation: Larger δ lowers the upper bound. The published family description states a positive, unspecified saving.

problems.assumptions: Unordered unit-distance pairs among n distinct points in the Euclidean plane. The exponent saving and multiplicative constant are absolute; this bound is distinct from the pinned-distances theorem.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes separately report a unit-distance bound with one fixed exponent β < 4/3 and a weak pinned-distances theorem. Neither description gives a numerical saving δ to rank.

papers.title: The weak pinned planar distance theorem
A power saving for planar unit distances

problems.publishedSummary: Proves the weak pinned Erdős distance conjecture: for every fixed ε > 0, all but $`o(n)`$ points of any n-point planar set determine at least $`n^{1-\varepsilon}`$ distinct nonzero distances. A complementary theorem bounds the number of unit-distance pairs by $`O(n^{4/3-\delta})`$ for an absolute δ > 0. ([Lean](lean/docs/167.md))

problems.name: Sidorenko counterexamples
problems.summary: Find a small bipartite pattern that appears less often than the random-graph prediction.
problems.why: The released manuscript challenges a long-standing prediction about how frequently patterns occur in networks, using one connected pattern with 35 vertices and 66 edges.
problems.opportunity: Seek a smaller valid counterexample pattern, or clarify which parts of the construction are necessary. A minimum within one finite template is not a minimum over all counterexamples.

metric.label: Counterexample-pattern vertices
metric.explanation: Smaller valid counterexample patterns would reduce the construction size. Internal counting constants and finite-template minima do not establish a smaller general counterexample.

problems.assumptions: A connected bipartite pattern H with 35 vertices and 66 edges, and a nonempty finite simple host graph G. Homomorphism density counts all vertex maps, not only injective copies. Smaller patterns require a valid analytic counterexample, not just a finite certificate in a chosen construction template.
problems.formalizationScope: The release notes report a finite host graph violating the Sidorenko density inequality for the fixed 35-vertex, 66-edge pattern. The separate forcing-conjecture consequence is outside that formalized statement. This app has not independently compiled the proof.

papers.title: A counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture

problems.publishedSummary: Disproves Sidorenko's conjecture with a connected bipartite pattern on 35 vertices and 66 edges that occurs less frequently than in a random graph of the same edge density. The same pattern disproves the forcing conjecture of Skokan and Thoma: matching its density and the edge density of a constant graphon need not force quasirandomness. ([Lean](lean/docs/161.md))

problems.name: Halving lines
problems.summary: Count lines through two points that leave equally many other points on each side.
problems.why: These counts are connected to geometric search and the complexity of separating point sets.
problems.opportunity: Make the positive exponent saving explicit or improve it, keeping the no-three-collinear assumption.

metric.label: Counting-exponent saving
metric.explanation: Larger ε gives fewer possible halving lines. The catalogue says the positive exponents are nonquantitative.

problems.assumptions: Even planar point sets with no three collinear, all sufficiently large sizes, and one absolute positive saving. A halving pair’s line leaves equally many remaining points on either side.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report halving-pair bounds and level-switch bounds with additional generic-position assumptions. The constants are existential, rather than numerical headline values.

papers.title: A power saving for planar halving lines

problems.publishedSummary: Improves the planar halving-line bound to $`O(n^{4/3-\varepsilon})`$ for sets with no three collinear and an absolute ε > 0. More generally, an n-point set with no three collinear has $`O(n(k+1)^{1/3-\varepsilon_0})`$ strictly separable k-subsets for $`1\le k\le n/2`$, with an absolute $`\varepsilon_0\gt 0`$. The constants and positive exponents are nonquantitative. ([Lean](lean/docs/183.md))

problems.name: Polynomial-free differences
problems.summary: How large can a set be while its pairwise gaps avoid values of a fixed polynomial?
problems.why: Quantitative size bounds describe how hard it is for a set to avoid this arithmetic structure.
problems.opportunity: Improve the saving cₖ for a fixed polynomial degree and preserve the required modular-root conditions.

metric.label: Size-exponent saving
metric.explanation: Larger cₖ gives a stronger upper bound on the set’s size. It depends on polynomial degree.

problems.assumptions: A fixed intersective integer polynomial h of degree k ≥ 2 with positive leading coefficient. Differences exclude nonzero positive-argument values; intersective means a root modulo every modulus. Prime-argument variants require a stronger modular condition.
problems.formalizationScope: The reported Lean statement is the square-difference case. The general intersective-polynomial and prime-argument claims in the family description have broader scope.

papers.title: A power saving for intersective polynomial differences with an exponent depending only on the degree
A Power Saving for Polynomial Differences at Prime Arguments
A power saving for square-difference-free sets

problems.publishedSummary: For every fixed intersective integer polynomial h of degree k ≥ 2 with positive leading coefficient, proves that a subset of $`\{1,\ldots,N\}`$ avoiding nonzero values $`h(1),h(2),\ldots`$ as differences has size $`O_h(N^{1-c_k})`$, with $`c_k\gt 0`$ depending only on degree. Here intersective means having a root modulo every modulus. For prime arguments, a power saving also holds when h has a unit root modulo every modulus, with exponent allowed to depend on h. ([Lean](lean/docs/182.md))

problems.name: Thin spanning trees
problems.summary: Connect a network with a tree that crosses every cut only a few times.
problems.why: A tree can be a sparse backbone of a larger network. The goal is to distribute its edges evenly across every possible separation.
problems.opportunity: Reduce the universal thinness constant C, preserving the connectivity and constructive guarantees.

metric.label: Thinness constant
metric.explanation: A smaller C is a thinner guaranteed tree. The overview gives no numerical value to compare.

problems.assumptions: Finite loopless k-edge-connected multigraphs with at least two vertices. Cuts count parallel edges with multiplicity, and the constructive runtime uses binary input length.
problems.formalizationScope: The notes report both an existential thin-tree bound and a separate deterministic polynomial-time construction. No numerical universal constant C is supplied.

papers.title: The strong thin tree conjecture
A polynomial-time construction of strong thin trees

problems.publishedSummary: Resolves the strong thin-tree conjecture constructively. Every finite loopless k-edge-connected multigraph on at least two vertices has a spanning tree containing at most a universal $`C/k`$ fraction of the edges of every cut. Such a tree can be found deterministically in polynomial time, even with binary-encoded parallel-edge multiplicities. ([Lean](lean/docs/174.md))

problems.name: Quantum-state approximations
problems.summary: Represent some two-dimensional quantum ground states using manageable mathematical building blocks.
problems.why: The released area-law manuscript claims polynomial bond-dimension approximations under a uniform spectral gap.
problems.opportunity: Improve the polynomial bond-dimension bound for the same gap, interactions, and approximation error.

metric.label: Bond-dimension growth
metric.explanation: A smaller growth exponent means a more compact representation. The constants depend on physical assumptions.

problems.assumptions: Unique ground states on open L×L squares, uniformly gapped nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians, bounded interactions, and global vector approximation error at most L⁻¹. Polynomial bond dimension is not a guarantee for arbitrary quantum states.
problems.formalizationScope: The catalogue does not list an accompanying top-line Lean formalization for this quantum-state approximation claim.

papers.title: A two-dimensional area law from a global spectral gap
Polynomial PEPS approximation of gapped square-grid ground states

problems.publishedSummary: Proves an entropy area law for unique ground states of finite-range Hamiltonians on arbitrary finite induced square-lattice domains, using only a uniform full-system spectral gap and bounds on the local interactions. On open $`L\times L`$ squares, uniformly gapped nearest-neighbor ground states also admit projected entangled-pair state approximations with polynomial bond dimension and global vector error at most L−1.

problems.name: Entangled-game repetition

The original manuscript establishes a bound of the form

$$W_r(k)>k^{c k\lfloor\log_2 r\rfloor}$$

# Sidorenko: finite-template minimum and a smaller residual bound

An independent, AI-generated research draft prepared with Codex, following OpenAI's *A counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture*. This repository contains two refinements of its method, proofs, exact certificates, and a reproducible enumeration.

**Scope:** a computer-assisted minimum within a specified finite construction template, and a smaller constant in one counting step. This is **not** a minimum for all Sidorenko counterexamples, a smaller general counterexample, or a verified bound on the full construction's dimension. The results depend on the stated source arguments and, for enumeration completeness, plantri. Mathematical priority and formal verification are not claimed.

## Results and proof ideas

### A 35-vertex minimum within the finite template

The template has distinct triangular faces; every point pair occurs in exactly two faces; each admissible cut partitions the faces into two spanning exposure orders; a probability distribution over cuts crosses every pair with probability at least $1/3$; and incidence color refinement, starting from the two part colors, is discrete.

Each exposure order builds a triangulated polygon containing every point on its boundary. Gluing the two polygons gives a sphere triangulation. Admissible cuts correspond to Hamiltonian cycles in its point graph. Consequently, if $a_e$ is the crossing probability,

$$\sum_{e\ni v}a_e=2.$$

Thus $a_e\ge1/3$ forces every point degree to be at most six. We enumerate all simple sphere triangulations on 4 through 12 points and filter by that condition and discrete incidence refinement:

| Points | All triangulations | Degree at most six | Discrete refinement | Exact obstructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| 7 | 5 | 5 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 14 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 50 | 15 | 1 | 1 |
| 10 | 233 | 30 | 4 | 4 |
| 11 | 1249 | 44 | 12 | 12 |
| 12 | 7595 | 77 | 23 | 23 |

For each surviving graph, the saved nonnegative rational edge weights sum to one and give **every Hamiltonian cycle weight strictly below $1/3$**. Any admissible cut mixture would instead have expected weight at least $1/3$, a contradiction. This excludes arbitrary weighted mixtures, not just three equally weighted cuts.

An independent exact verifier uses Held–Karp dynamic programming, checks 16,941 cycles in aggregate, and obtains a minimum separating margin of $1/75$. The original 13-point, 22-face certificate gives the matching 35-vertex incidence graph. Completeness remains dependent on plantri's enumeration algorithm; the certificates are not Lean proofs.

At 13 points, a further enumeration leaves exactly two feasible isomorphism classes within the finite template. One is the original; the other is a different 35-vertex finite certificate. Both pass the combinatorial and support checks. **The alternative is not claimed as a newly proved counterexample:** its full analytic transfer has not been independently verified.

### Residual constant: 1641 to 1032

The original proof's equality stratum forces zero pair dimension wherever cut coverage exceeds $1/3$. Its published cuts exclude five pairs, leaving only 28 potentially active pairs. This tightens the local dimension caps.

Writing $d=\sum_i k_i-2k\ge1$, the original counting exponent, including the gain, is bounded by

$$-Dd-k^2+2mk-2m+\sum_i\binom{k_i}{2}.$$

The new caps first bound the remainder by 1196. For $d=1$, a convexity bound and 54 exact integer cases improve it to 1032; $d\ge2$ is already covered by the coarser bound. Thus this nondirect residual contribution is

$$O_D(q^{-D+1032})\qquad(D\ge1032).$$

Even dimension **1034**, instead of 1642, suffices for this one step. Earlier residue and transverse thresholds remain required and may dominate. The graph, cuts, and activation laws are unchanged.

## Reproduce

Use Python 3.11 or 3.12:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -B run_checks.py
```

GitHub Actions runs the same command on pushes and pull requests. Do not enable Python optimization (`-O` or `PYTHONOPTIMIZE`); certificate assertions must remain active. The runner rejects optimized execution.

The full argument is in [proof.tex](proof.tex), which has been compiled successfully with the Codex document editor. No compiled PDF is bundled. The tests supplement the mathematical argument; they are not a formal proof of the original papers or an independent review.

The Sidorenko runner also requires a C compiler (`cc`, or set `CC`) and network access to retrieve one hash-verified original source file. It builds the included unmodified plantri source into ignored `build/`, reruns the enumeration through 13 points, checks the saved certificates independently, verifies the original finite certificate, and recomputes the residual bound from the original published table. Outputs go to `build/`; the saved evidence is preserved.

## Evidence and tests

- [Exact obstruction witnesses](experiments/cut-obstructions/summary.json), [independent minimum check](experiments/minimality-independent.json).
- [Order-13 classification](experiments/order-13-classification-independent.json) and [two feasible certificates](experiments/order-13-cuts/).
- [Residual arithmetic expectations](experiments/residual-expected.json), including every span case.
- [verify_minimality.py](verify_minimality.py) reconstructs faces and refinement separately from the proposal code and optimizes Hamiltonian-cycle weights exactly, without SciPy.
- [check_complex.py](check_complex.py) checks pair multiplicity, connectedness, exposure orders, coverage, refinement, and support intersections. Duplicate-face and incomplete-exposure mutations are rejected.
- A corrupted edge-weight certificate is rejected. Floating-point LP success or failure is never used as the final infeasibility certificate.

To regenerate proposed witnesses, install `requirements-search.txt` and use `certify_cut_obstructions.py --help`. The included optimizer uses SciPy only to suggest rational witnesses; the independent verifier certifies them. `enumerate_triangulations.py` and `search_complex.py` retain the proposal methods for inspection.

- [plantri 5.8](https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/plantri/), by Gunnar Brinkmann, Heidi Van den Camp, and Brendan McKay, supplies the enumeration. Its unmodified C source, manual, [Apache 2.0 license](vendor/plantri/LICENSE-2.0.txt), and [download provenance](vendor/plantri/provenance.json) are included. The saved verification receipt pins the C-source hash.

This repository is an independent follow-up, not an official OpenAI publication.

## Argument

The source obtains equations

$$2(p_i-r_\ell)\cdot(H_i-U_\ell)=R_{i\ell}(A_i-A'_\ell),\qquad A_i-A'_\ell\ne0.$$

Let $J(x,y)=(-y,x)$, $v=r_2-r_1$, and

$$\omega=\frac{(U_2-U_1)\cdot Jv}{v\cdot v}.$$

The denominator is nonzero because the anchors are distinct real points at the finite indices. Subtract a common translation and infinitesimal rotation from all velocities, and subtract $A'_1$ from all logarithmic velocities:

$$\widetilde H_i=H_i-U_1-\omega J(p_i-r_1),\qquad \widetilde U_\ell=U_\ell-U_1-\omega J(r_\ell-r_1).$$

The equations are preserved since $x\cdot Jx=0$. The first right velocity and first logarithmic velocity become zero, while the second right velocity is parallel to $v$. Nine generic left points therefore guarantee a point surviving as generic after those generators are adjoined. The source's private valuations make the radical square classes independent. # Matrix multiplication: a barrier for symmetrized sector inequalities

An independent, AI-generated research draft prepared with Codex. We construct an explicit abstract profile satisfying the retained scalar constraints from OpenAI's matrix-multiplication manuscript, then show that it also survives arbitrary numbers of standard matched sectors with unequal lengths.

**This is a limitation of a specified proof method, not a new matrix-multiplication algorithm, a lower bound on the actual exponent, or a proof that 9/4 is optimal.** The profile is not claimed to be realizable by a tensor character. Mathematical priority, independent review, and formal verification are not claimed.

## Explicit profile

For $a,b\ge1$, put $u=\min(a,b)$ and $v=\max(a,b)$. Define

```math
P_*(a,b)=\left(\frac{3u-1}{2}\right)^{1/3}\left(v+\frac{u-1}{2}\right).
```

The proof shows positivity, symmetry, monotonicity, separate concavity, the boundary value $P_*(1,b)=b$, shifted tripling, and the rank envelope at $t=3/4$:

```math
P_*(a,3h+a-1)\ge3P_*(a,h),\qquad P_*(a,b)\le(a+b-1)^{4/3}.
```

Yet its diagonal grows only as

```math
P_*(a,a)=\left(\frac{3a-1}{2}\right)^{4/3}=\Theta(a^{4/3}).
```

Thus those abstract constraints alone cannot exclude $t=3/4$ or force a larger diagonal power.

## Why unequal and additional standard sectors do not remove this obstruction

Suppose $C(a,B)$ degenerates to $s$ standard polynomial-multiplication blocks $C(a,h_i)$ sharing the first leg, with independent second and third legs. Allow an exchange of those two legs in each block, but no auxiliary output factors. Counting the two spaces forces

```math
B\ge\sum_i h_i+\lfloor s/2\rfloor(a-1).
```

Using a common probability vector across the six permuted characters, the source's entropy inequality yields the symmetrized consequence

```math
P(a,B)\ge\sum_iP(a,h_i).
```

The profile above satisfies every such consequence. Indeed, writing $d=(a-1)/2$ and $L=((3a-1)/2)^{1/3}$ gives $P_*(a,h)\le L(h+d)$, with equality for $h\ge a$. The needed dominance reduces, after cubing positive quantities, to

```math
A(A+2H)^3-H(2A+H)^3=(A-H)^3(A+H)\ge0\qquad(A\ge H).
```

The dimension bound then implies the desired sum inequality. See [proof.tex](proof.tex) for both complete analytic arguments.
